utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice to continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for there to be a prospect of my concluding today, first it will be necessary for me to sacrifice to a degree maybe the appearance of a completely chronological approach. I'll do my best. Second, I will invite the Chamber at the first break, should it indicate that it might be willing to take this course, to review one or possibly two documents. The first document is the typed comments, now both in English and B/C/S, provided by Professor Kristan on the constitutional matters that were raised, and in light of what the Chamber postulated as a possibility that he be recalled, it may be that it will be helpful and time saving to read those -- that document. It's four or five pages in English. And I would also invite the Chamber, or may also invite the Chamber if I've got sufficiently far advanced in the questions I wish to ask, to review the critical document that I provided to the witness yesterday for him to review, because again, the criticisms contained there are criticisms that would form the subject of my cross-examination and pre-reading might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No doubt he would have read that document over night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that in terms of time, the Trial Chamber has been rebuked for trespassing on the time of another Trial Chamber. Quite often we go beyond 1.45 and that interferes with the trial which is to start, so we are not to do that. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, I'm just going to return to a couple of matters that we dealt with yesterday, but first I want to return immediately to the question of the constitutions that you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you issue an order to have these same documents handed to me? For example, I did not receive the same documents that Professor Markovic received yesterday. I hope I will receive that as well as the one that Mr. Nice just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you should receive that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should have received that. Are the documents available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're certainly available, yes. They can be provided. Kristan in B/C/S will be a few minutes, but other than that, of course they can be available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, I want to turn to your assistance in respect of constitutions that you drafted, because you gave answers yesterday rejecting the suggestion that you had assisted at all in the drafting of either a constitution for the Republika Srpska or for the Republic of Serb Krajina and identified, it seemed, the constitution of Montenegro as perhaps the missing constitution, but this is exactly what you said when asked questions by this accused and a follow-up question by His Honour Judge Robinson. You said: "I can't enumerate them all. I can tell you the names of three but not the fourth. One was the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, the 1991; the constitution of the Republic of Montenegro, the 1992 one, in October; and the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia dating to 1992. I still come under the Official Secrets Act, so I can't quote you the fourth country." Now, will you please name the fourth country.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to correct you, because you keep making mistakes in your questions. First of all, I did not say that I wrote the drafts of these constitutions. And please do not manipulate this particular type of wording yet again. I did not do the writing. I was on a team that did the writing, so it was a collective effort. Secondly, I never mentioned any Official Secrets Act, nor am I aware of any such act or law. I spoke of professional privilege. Mr. Nice, I am -- I do not have to tell anyone as to what I do in my profession. There is full freedom in this respect in my country. I can write whatever I wish to write, but they are adopted or not adopted by competent bodies. Perhaps I am writing a constitution or a law right now, working on that kind of thing. Why are you interested in that? You are entering the realm of the private in this way, and you have no right to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, the words "Official Secrets Act" come straight off the transcript, so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter who said that notes that it might have been "privileged information" but at the speed we were going, that is the first term that came to mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that would be a sterile debate into which to enter because the position has been clarified. All the witness is claiming is professional privilege, and as far as I'm concerned, he doesn't have that here to refuse to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I now assist you with something else, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not seeking an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am, certainly, and I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, before I turn to my next point on this, you've heard His Honour's observation about whether privilege exists of the kind you claim. Will you please name the other -- fourth country to which you referred.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Jovicic and I together worked on the statute of the Serb Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this the Serb Autonomous Region that you yesterday told me had no constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember you made a very clever remark -- not clever remark, not for me to qualify it. A remark about, was it Lord Palmerston when you challenged me to show you a document? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... existence of something you knew well to exist, Professor Markovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lord Palmerston said to a British MP who invoked the British constitution, he said that he was prepared to give a handsome reward to anyone who gave him that kind of information. What I did was not a constitution. It was a constitutional document. We as professionals were asked to do it. So that's why I said if you show me the constitution, that was the statute of the autonomous region. Of course it is a document of constitutional nature but nevertheless it is not a constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, you knew from my questions yesterday that I was interested in establishing that you had assisted in the drafting of the constitutions of the Republic of Serb Krajina and the Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. As a matter of fact, it's a lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my questions. What was I trying to discover from you? You tell the Court, please, so that we can understand your thinking process, and let me not beat about the bush, so that we can see whether you're an honest man. What was the purpose of my question, Professor Markovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I know? You're the one who should know. How can I know what the point of your question is? For me these questions are pointless, but you probably know why you're putting them to me. These questions have nothing to do with my evidence. I have been giving evidence about completely different matters, whereas you are working ad hominem. You are analysing me as a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, the questions go to your credibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to give you one last chance before we move on. What you did yesterday was an attempt deliberately to mislead this Court about your involvement in the drafting constitutions for the RSK and the RS. Could you explain, please, why.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I never wrote or participated in writing the two constitutions that you mentioned. Never. Only the statute of the Serb Autonomous Region. As a matter of fact, Republika Srpska has so many learned professors of constitutional law that they themselves are in a position to help draft a constitution. Why would they engage me from Belgrade when they already have such people in their own midst?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll take no further time of this witness, and the Court will be probably pleased to learn I'm now determined to try and finish him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, could you clarify for me what you mean in that answer by the reference to the "Serb Autonomous Region."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb Autonomous Region in the sense of "oblast." "Oblast" is the word I used, not "pokrajina," the one that was created in Croatia. Since there weren't any legal professionals, at that time Professor Jovicic and I were asked to do it in order to stylize the norms. It simply has to do with craftsmanship, how to draft norms and standards. Of course, the ideas have to be those that are set out in the first place. I can write a constitution for Zanzibar if somebody tells me what kind of social system they want, what the history of Zanzibar, because I do it as a craftsman. I draft the norms. I do not create the constitution from the point of view of the underlying ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Court will be interested to recall that in the evidence of Mr. Babic, initially protected but like so much of his evidence subsequently released from any protection, he was asked about the statute, constitution, and he said, when asked who drafted it, he said it was drafted by Borivoj Rasua and Professor Ratko Markovic. I turn to another topic out of sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You concluded your work on the amendments to the Serb constitution and the Kosovo constitution and the Vojvodina constitution in the spring of 1989. Just one thing before I move to my next short topic. After the Kosovo Assembly passed in the manner it did those amendments, people died on the streets in demonstrations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I am quite unaware of that. I'm not from Kosovo, and I did not follow events on the spot. I think it is quite irrelevant for me to recount what I read in the newspapers at that time, and that was 24 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... relevant. We've had evidence of deaths on the streets, and my question to you, and it's going to apply to all your evidence today, is this: As someone involved - and we've seen the terms of your approval - someone involved in making such dramatic changes to the constitutional arrangements of the former Yugoslavia, do you feel any responsibility for the things that happened, such as those deaths on the streets of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two cannot be related at all. As a matter of fact, I have great professional pride that I took part in all of this, and I consider it to be one of my greatest professional achievements that I took part in that particular endeavour. And the fact that somebody is trying to turn a province into a state and investing his own life in it has nothing to do with my professional work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't accept that characterisation of what happened, but we'll move on. In 1990, the SPS was formed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for you to say. It's your own affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the accused's party was formed, and something you haven't told us about is that you were a founding member of that party, on its Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, for four months. And since I lost the elections in order to win a seat in parliament, I resigned because I thought that the party had lost with me on the ticket, and I thought that the party did not benefit from my presence. And since then I was nothing but an ordinary member of the SPS. I tendered my resignation guided by the democratic principle that whoever loses an election has to suffer the consequences, and therefore, I resigned my membership on the Executive Board. I was a member from July to December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, ever since 1990, I repeat, I have been nothing but an ordinary member of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, an ordinary member of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A member of the group that discussed the division of Bosnia following the Karadjordjevo meeting of Milosevic and Tudjman, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it, from you now. Could you tell me more specifically what you're referring to? What you're saying is pure science fiction. I have no idea what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the famous meeting of the accused and Tudjman at Karadjordjevo where they discussed the partitioning of Bosnia, working groups were set up on either side to deal with the putting into effect of possible agreements. You were a member of the group serving Milosevic, this accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice cannot include in his question an assertion that I talked to Tudjman about the division of Bosnia. That is just something that he is claiming, and of course it is false. He gives an assertion, "when they discussed the division of Bosnia," et cetera, et cetera. He can ask him what he did, but that is not a fact that he can proceed from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is part of Mr. Nice's case. It's part of the Prosecution case, and if I'm not mistaken, evidence was led to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson, that meeting was just between me and Tudjman in accordance with the evidence that you have. So referring to the evidence is senseless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not appropriate to comment now. Evidence of that meeting has been given, and it's on that basis that the question is being put. At the end of the day, it will be a matter for the Chamber to assess the evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, in the time that's passed following the accused's observations, have you now remembered your participation in this group that advised this accused? The first meeting was held in the hunting castle near Osijek on the 10th of April of 1991. Think back.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a working group, not a team that served Milosevic. Please, I have to react to such wording. You're a lawyer just like I am. You cannot put it that way that I served Milosevic. It was a working group that included Academician Kosta Mihailovic, Professor Smilja Avramov, Professor Vladan Kutlesic, and myself. On the other side there was Dusan Bilandzic as leader. He's a professor and an academician too, and then also a constitutional lawyer like myself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness will have to slow down. The interpreters cannot follow at this speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have lost the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note again that the speaking is moving too fast, mentioning names. If you wish to have an accurate transcript, we cannot do it at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, the interpreter has just made a comment that you're speaking too fast, mentioning several names. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I do apologise. It is a professional deformity, because I try to say as much as possible during my classes. So this was a working group on which was Academician Kosta Mihailovic, Professor Smilja Avramov, Professor Vladan Kutlesic, and myself. On the other side, our partners in these talks were Academician Dusan Bilandzic -- I'm not sure whether he's an academician but I think he is, a member of the academy. Professor Smiljko Sokol, Professor Zvonko Lerotic, and I cannot remember who the fourth member was. My partner for these talks was Professor Smiljko Sokol who teaches constitutional law in Zagreb just like I teach it in Belgrade, but I'm saying to you that if you think that university professors divide Bosnia, you are overestimating professors. Professors never divide territories. It is only the top political echelons that can do that kind of thing anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course you were an ordinary member of the SPS, and since you mention one of the members of the other side, let's see what he had to say about it, please. If we can have a look at this next exhibit. Please take the -- as it comes your way, take the B/C/S version of the newspaper article from Nacional, the 26th -- the 25th of October, 1996, and if the usher would be good enough to display the English language version of this document, you will see about this meeting. This is how your colleague on the other side described things, Professor. This is from --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who is this colleague?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bilandzic. There's a picture of him. And you'll find the following text --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honours will give me one minute. I wasn't expecting to have to deal with it necessarily at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'd look, please, Professor, on the second of the sheets of the newspaper. Second sheet of the newspaper, left-hand column, at the foot under the cross-heading "Najveca Razilazenja," we see the following: "However, the biggest disagreements Tudjman and I had were in discussions about Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the beginning of 1991, after his negotiations with Milosevic, it was agreed that two commissions were to meet and discuss the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tudjman told us then that he and Milosevic came to an agreement in principle and that we were to work out the concrete details on maps. Academy member Kosta Mihailovic, chief of the cabinet of Milosevic, Kupresic, Smilja Avramov, and the vice-president of the government of Serbia were participants in these discussions from the Serbian side. Three ten-hour rounds of talks were held in Tikves and in Belgrade. However, these talks yielded no results." I return to my original question to you: Were you a member of a group or team, however you prefer to describe it, that took part in discussions with your opposing numbers to consider the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the team, but the division of Bosnia was not discussed at all. What was discussed were general problems that the country was facing and how we professional people viewed this from our professional point of view. As for Bosnia, divisions, looking at maps, heaven forbid, there was no mention of that. No participant can say any such thing. They're all alive. They can all tell you that no partition of Bosnia was ever referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me invite you to reconsider that last answer in light of the following: You say "heaven forbid," reference to maps. Your colleague Smilja Avramov has given evidence before this Court, and she spoke in quite specific terms about working with maps. So think back, Professor. Tell us what the maps had to do with your meetings.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was ever any mention of maps and that any maps were shown at all. No maps at all whatsoever at those meetings were brought up. It was a tete-a-tete meeting, one-on-one, and everyone was able to present their own visions of the crisis that the country was in and the ways out of that crisis. There was not a single word about the division of Bosnia, not one single word. And that is what I claim and I have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth here. So there was not a single word about Bosnia, and I only went to Bosnia two or three times in my life, so I'm not competent enough to speak about it. I don't know the towns and places in Bosnia where the -- what kind of population lives in what area, so how could I be competent enough to speak about Bosnia at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you should seek to find out whether you're talking about the same meeting. If you're able to pinpoint the membership, the professor can say whether he identified with those persons at meetings, whether he worked with those persons at the meeting. It may be that he's talking about a different meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I can deal with that. The accused had something he wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to say that Smilja Avramov, Professor Smilja Avramov never testified about having worked on some project to divide Bosnia between Croatia and Serbia. That's completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. And I didn't suggest otherwise. She gave a different account of the meetings, but she was constrained to accept that she was working with maps. This witness denied fulsomely working with maps at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to tidy that matter up, although again I had hoped not to take this time --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, where do you see my name here? Quote it if you can. Go on, say where my name appears here, if you can, since you're operating with this exhibit. Just show me where my name is there if you can find. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I, of course, don't respond to approaches like that by the witness and it might be thought to be an inappropriate approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but it was also the point of my comment earlier as to whether you're talking about the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another document. Perhaps the usher would be good enough. I'm afraid -- this is extract from Smilja Avramov's book where indeed she sticks to her account that there was no reference to division of Bosnia. Let's just look at what she does say, because the witness wants to see his name cited as a member of the group. What she said was this. English version on the overhead projector. Thank you very much. "The presidents of the two republics, Tudjman and Milosevic, took another step, but this time one of the informal nature; they formed two teams in order to unanimously consider the political, economic, constitutional law and the international law consequences of a possible disintegration of Yugoslavia and to find a solution through that prism. It is likely that the decision on that matter was made at a meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction here. In the Serbian translation, I heard that they formed two teams so that they could unanimously view. It's not a question of unanimously viewing, "jednoglasno," in Serbian. They set up two teams with the aim of comprehensively reviewing the political, et cetera, et cetera, consequences of a possible disintegration of Yugoslavia and through that prism to seek solutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We accept that correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I read on: "It's likely that the decision on that matter was made at a meeting of the two leaders in Karadjordjevo in March 1991, but no one informed the group of the development and the results of those meetings. Footnote 14. The negotiating group on the Croatian side consisted of President Tudjman's advisors Josip Sentija and Dusan Bilandzic, and the professors at the University of Zagreb, Zvonko Lerotic and Smiljko Sokol. The Serbian group was comprised of President Milosevic's advisors; an Academician Kosta Mihajlovic and Vladan Kutlesic, and professors of Belgrade University Ratko Markovic and Smilja Avramov. The first meeting was held in a hunting castle near Osijek on the 10th of April, the second meeting in Dedinje on the 13th of April, and the third meeting in Zagreb a week later." Let's go back to the topic I was about to leave. You were a member of this group referred to by Smilja Avramov and also by Dusan Bilandzic in the Nacional newspaper article that we've read, weren't you? One and the same group.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same working group; however, I did not attend that third meeting in Zagreb myself. I was there on the 10th of April and the 13th of April, but the third in Zagreb -- on the third in Zagreb, a week later, I did not attend that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you seem to have a good active recollection of these meetings, or did you only recover your recollection of them when prompted by these documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you all this before. Everything you've read out to me I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think that this is highly improper because the witness is being led astray. It is being suggested that he took part in a working group on the division of Bosnia. What is being read out here now with Smilja Avramov makes no mention of the division of Bosnia. It deals with general issues and a comprehensive review of all questions of importance to the Yugoslav crisis. There is not a single mention of Bosnia. And here, in the quotation that we had a moment ago, he says none of the attempts succeeded. The only point - and this was something that Mr. Nice quoted - on which the two sides agreed was the -- that the main determinant for talks was to be 70 years of life in common. All other attitudes were far apart on all other issues. So he's asking the witness about the division of Bosnia and shows that there was a group of intellectuals who exchanged views and opinions by comprehensively reviewing the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I consider your point to be a fair one. It had occurred to me. Mr. Nice, what this witness has said is that he did not participate in any meeting in which maps were used, did not discuss the division of Bosnia. The document that you have cited does not speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that I neither accepted the account given as to the detail of the meeting when advanced by Smilja Avramov, nor by this witness. On the contrary, the Prosecution case is reflected in the version given by the interlocutor on the other side, Bilandzic. But as to this witness, he sought, I will argue in due course, really to deny participation at all in these meetings, and the witness Avramov made it quite clear that borders were considered and maps were used, and it will be for the Chamber in due course to decide, putting all that evidence together, where the truth lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think you can take the matter any further. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask, however, that both these documents, the newspaper report and the extract from Smilja Avramov's book, be exhibited, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is the Avramov book not part of the evidence already?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Our recollection -- I'm sorry if I overlooked it. Our recollection is that it hadn't been produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is the status of the newspaper report which hasn't been confirmed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a species of hearsay evidence. If there's any doubt as to that being the views of this witness, we can deal with that -- not this witness. That being -- there being any doubt as to that being the views of the speaker referred to in the newspaper, we can deal with it in a number of ways, not least, of course, by seeking to call him in rebuttal. But I would ask that the newspaper be admitted at this stage. We will, of course, add him, or can add him to list B so that we remember to consider him as a witness we may wish to call later, but it is like so much of the other material that's been put in, prima facie evidence of its truth and a species of acceptable hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're back to a problem. Certainly it's a problem I have and I may be alone in this, I'm not sure, but it's the timing of the presentation of this that concerns me. You call it hearsay and that may be a proper description of it, and it may well in an appropriate context be admissible hearsay, but we're in the Defence phase of the case, we're not in the Prosecution phase of the case, and therefore there has to be some way in which it's accepted by the witness before it can have any status. On the other hand, I see the point you make about the potential need to rebut some evidence, and if that's right and you can justify it in due course, is it not then that the question of exhibition arises?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand Your Honour's concerns. In each case, the problem arises -- in most cases it arises in the same structural way as it arises here: The Prosecution puts in its case not knowing fully the degree of challenge that there's going to be, so that here primary evidence was given, and extensive evidence, from Ante Markovic, from President Mesic, and so on, of the content of the Karadjordjevo meeting. The accused calls now two witnesses, Smilja Avramov and this witness, who were members of the committee that -- or the group or the team that set to work either in implementation of or in consideration of that primary agreement. They give evidence that the Prosecution doesn't accept, and doesn't accept for good reason because it has evidence or material to the contrary effect, inter alia, the primary evidence and the secondary evidence, for example, coming as to the subordinate meetings in this newspaper article. It wouldn't have been reasonable or necessary or appropriate to put in all such newspaper articles and material as part of our case, and it might have been difficult for us to do so. It would be inappropriate for us not to draw this material to your attention when it's contrary to the defendant's case, and it may be appropriate for us to call the evidence in rebuttal. But here we come to the practical problems of cases of this kind and size. If -- if we deal with this with every conceivable point and try and call it in rebuttal, we'll almost certainly be arguing for a rebuttal case larger than the Chamber would want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But my impression, Mr. Nice, is that when this type of material was offered by the Defence in the course of the Prosecution case, it wasn't regularly exhibited because its provenance and its reliability were questionable. And what you've produced is a photocopy of a newspaper report of what someone said. And I have to say that I would have reservations about anyone claiming in a court that he was relying on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what was supposed to have said reported in a newspaper, without some sort of evidence to support the circumstances and context of how it's suggested I came to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, beginning with the two points that arise from that. I think in the Prosecution's case, as we've indicated in our recent filing, there were -- there was a broad test for admissibility, and I think documents of this kind did find their way in from time to time at the hands of the accused but I would need a moment of time to find some particular examples. And I would press the Chamber, in light of the particular difficulties that these cases present, to consider this material and indeed to admit it at this stage, because it's important that you should know material contrary to the evidence of a witness such as this exists. And we can consider not least by identifying the witness on our list B of potential additional witnesses, we can decide later on the need to prove this in strict evidential terms or possibly not to rely on this material, if that were to be our decision, if it's not further corroborated by other similar material between now and the end of the Defence case. But it would be unfortunate not to have the material, and in our submission unnecessary not to have the material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Thanks very much. Let me hear from Mr. Kay and then the accused briefly on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It would be fortunate for Mr. Nice to have this material in rather than unfortunate for the trial process. What he should be doing is putting in evidence that is either adopted by the witness so it has an evidentiary foundation or exhibits from his own case. What we're having now, and there's been a tendency throughout the Defence to have documents wheeled out from other reports, other sources, which apparently go to an issue, that he wants to use the Defence process of the trial, the Defence phase of the trial as a means of getting that evidence in to build up his case without the actual evidence itself having become evidence in the trial proceedings. And he has had 300 days to present a case, and in that time produced thousands, many thousands of exhibits on issues relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he says it's hearsay evidence, which is admissible under our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hearsay evidence is admissible, but it has -- it has to be evidence in some form. This is just a document which doesn't even mention this accused, as I've been through it carefully and sometimes you miss things, but I can't see his name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It mentions the accused. It doesn't mention the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's certainly difficult for me to tell because I suspect the English is not a translation of the full -- the full article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've been looking at the B/C/S text behind which is very -- it's of small typeface and I can't see it there either. So that this extract doesn't mention the witness, the witness disagrees with what's being said, you're asked to consider it as an exhibit in the case because it contains a contrary view. Well, we've had the contrary view. That lasted 300 days. It's now the Defence phase of the case. Evidence can become admissible if adopted, but the danger is that you're going to be building up here a bank of material of no provenance, of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it's hearsay evidence that's admissible under our Rules, that is to say if it meets reliability tests and so on, isn't the only issue then one of authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not even hearsay evidence. It's not what someone said to someone who's a witness in the case. This man has never been a witness in the case. It's something he said to a journalist on another occasion. It's not even in the category of evidential material of the trial, but it contains an apparently contrary point of view favourable to one side. If it was evidence admissible in that form, it should have come in in their case and have some kind of justification, but we're at the stage of the Defence case now, where the witness says, "Well, I disagree with that and that's not true," and something's being put in where we don't even know if this man agrees to this interview or accepts it. It's just a piece of paper. It's not even hearsay evidence, in my submission. It doesn't -- sorry, Your Honour Judge Kwon, if I can just finish. In an investigative process where all materials may be collected, which is an entirely different concept from the one we're dealing with now and where you more rightly control what's looked at, then it may have some kind of evidential foundation, but in these proceedings and at this stage it does not. Sorry, Judge Kwon. I know you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Another issue may be the consistency of our practice, or equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the Prosecution's case, was it not the practice that the Defence was not allowed to present this kind of evidence on the ground that he could call the witness during his case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly so. For the -- there were occasions when some documents were put in which carried with them a major point, though -- I can't remember now off the -- standing on my feet. There were some occasions and the practice was against it and firm rulings were made and Mr. Milosevic was told firmly, "Well, your chance to produce the evidence will come." And as I say, it would be fortunate for Mr. Nice if this went in because his chance to call evidence has gone, and if he does want a rebuttal case containing this material, those are decisions that he has to make, if he wants to call this witness and have him adopt the material. But it's not anything connected with this particular witness giving evidence at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if I may say so, I think you hit upon a point which has been troubling me about our -- the nature of our proceedings here. It's the conflict or the potential conflict between the two legal systems. You mentioned that it would be admissible if it were the investigative, civil law type of procedure, but I have had to retrain myself since I came here. I'm from the common law system, and I think I have eventually succeeded in accepting that admissibility of evidence is on the more relaxed mode in the civil law inquisitorial system, although the presentation of evidence follows the adversarial system. And it is because I am being influenced by that why I would tend to think that it is -- it's admissible. But I'd like to -- I think we would reserve on this particular point and consider it and give a decision on the admissibility later, because we also have to consider the question raised by Judge Kwon of consistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are dangers -- if I may just mention. There are dangers in thinking that when something happens, oh, well it might well fall into the other system. Again, provenance in the investigative system is important as well, and there's a review of the file. You're actually being asked to short circuit that here and now and make this an exhibit, not even marked for identification to give the opportunity for a witness to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I should hear Mr. Milosevic very briefly on this doctrinal point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, Mr. Robinson, that this is quite nonsensical, because not even somebody who grants an interview testifies about that but does so by the by, by the way, in passing. He takes an example of how he was, for example, good friends with Tudjman. Look at what it says. It says Bilandzic, the man Bilandzic is responding to accusations which in his last interview was presented by Tudjman to the media. And then it goes on to say Tudjman went -- was too hasty, a monster, and they were friends in the 1950s. And then to impress the public about that fact, of having been friends, he says, "Well, I even drew up maps with the Serbs about the division of Bosnia." That's what he says, which isn't true, and you can see that from the book. The book is not a yellow press interview; it is a book written by Professor Avramov and speaks about the fact that they discussed the situation in Yugoslavia in a comprehensive manner, nothing to do with the division of Bosnia. This is not even secondhand, hearsay evidence. And if Mr. Nice wants to prove this through Bilandzic, who was the Croatian ambassador to Belgrade at one point, well, why doesn't he bring Bilandzic in to testify? What does it mean, presenting us with completely worthless papers like this? And he had the possibility of bringing them in. And he had the time. Has twice the number of days accorded to him that I have for my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That part is not true. That part is not true, and we have been through that before. You will be given the same time as the Prosecutor had. What we will do is we will set aside this document and other documents of that kind which the Prosecutor is seeking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me finish. We'll set aside those documents and reserve our position on their admissibility to a later stage. We will exhibit the Avramov document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I make one final observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up simply on His Honour Judge Kwon's point about practice in the Prosecution case. Where words of the kind recalled by Judge Kwon were used, saying, "You can call the witness in the Defence case," and of course I remember such words being used and indeed on several or many occasions, it was in the recognition that there was a -- effectively an open opportunity for the accused to call witnesses. The realities of the potential to call a rebuttal witness are different because in real terms one knows that there will be substantial limits on the rebuttal case. And so where a new topic is called, that is the topic of the groups serving the initial Karadjordjevo meeting, not only is it our right to identify contrary material, and possibly our duty to present it in some form, but I would ask you to say that in the particular circumstances, that justifies admissibility. That's all I would add to my earlier argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, we may be able to apply a more lenient rule in relation to the rebuttal case, having come from the civil law countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour mean more lenient in the sense of more permissive in the calling of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For that, of course, many thanks as the advocate of the cause, but I recognise the problems that will have for the timetable. Can I move on to another topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this one in fact is going to kick off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Avramov document is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be 817.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you like to give the MFI to Kosovo, Law and Politics which was tendered yesterday in court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we should. We should.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So that would be 818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic wanted to say something. Not on the question of allocation of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you said that I had stated something that was not truthful, and I don't think that it is untruthful that Mr. Nice had 300 days and I am to have only 150 days. This is a fact that is known to everyone. Therefore, 300 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I disallowed that kind of question, that kind of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Should the questioned document be given an MFI number so that it fits in the sequence of events, rather than come out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps another kind of notation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All marked-for-identification exhibits are subject to a decision of the Chamber in due course as to whether they are admitted or rejected, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So it will be 819.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, I'm moving on, and to remind us, we were exploring in the most general terms your role in events. I'll have to come back and deal with the drafting of constitutions, but we know that you became a Deputy Prime Minister for five or six years, was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was Deputy Prime Minister in the cabinet for six and a half years. I served two terms in two governments. The second term was not a full one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On any reckoning being one of the three Deputy Prime Ministers is to place you at the heart of the administration, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I've said several times so far that there were five Deputy Prime Ministers, not three. So there were five of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be one of five Deputy Prime Ministers places you at the heart of the administration?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the Deputy Prime Minister is not regulated in the law on the cabinet. Deputy Prime Minister can stand in for the Prime Minister if he's for some reason absent. And in addition to that, Deputy Prime Minister carries out tasks given to him by the Prime Minister. I was given a task to be in charge of the legislation and legal system of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you retained your position as a professor at the faculty in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I continued to be a university professor. I served for six and a half years as Deputy Prime Minister on a pro bono basis. I received no salary for that. My only income came from my salary of university professor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of your fellow -- oh, yes. You got your position as Deputy Prime Minister because of your membership in the SPS party, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some Deputy Prime Ministers who were not members of the SPS. For example, Slobodan Radulovic, in charge of commerce, was a member of the New Democracy Party. Svetozar Krstic was Deputy Prime Minister in charge of economy. He was a member of the New Democracy Party. That was in the second -- first term. And in the second term there were even more non-SPS members as Deputy Prime Ministers than SPS ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed so. One of them was Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the second determine, lasting from 1998. At the time, he was one of the five Deputy Prime Ministers. I believe he was in charge of the economy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he had the good fortune to be appointed as a full professor at your faculty, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected for a tenured professor based on a paper prepared by a three-member commission and based on the appointment which was carried out in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now look at how you were reported, and this comes from a media outlet, I think indeed it may have been taken off the internet, but can we see how you were reported to have approached Vojislav Seselj's professorship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document coming the way of the Court is Vreme weekly of the 15th of April of 2000. If the usher could display the English version on the overhead projector, providing the -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, on the first sheet of the B/C/S, under the heading Odabrana Bibliografija, about ten lines down there's a sentence beginning, "Tako je..." The article itself, as we can see in the newspaper format, asked whether the Deputy Prime Minister was on the committee for writing - that's you - were on the committee for writing reports on applicants to help in the election of Vojislav Seselj as professor. And your quoted words, and I want to know if these are accurately quoted, are these: "... his works are of unbalanced level of depth, but author's knowledge in the field of political theory, philosophy and history cannot be denied, as well as, possession of information, sharp and literate expression and polemical style, general knowledge and almost passionate dedication to subjects about which he writes ... Dr. Vojislav Seselj masterfully rules the public scene, which is demonstrated in countless public appearances at public debates, television and radio, public lectures, political campaigning ... The crystal clarity of his publicly spoken words, logic in making conclusions, rich lexica and almost perfect intonation of his speech are a guarantee that Dr. Vojislav Seselj will always be an interesting lecturer that students would gladly listen to ... The content and number of his published, expert and technical works, stunning rhetorical gift and suggestiveness of his address to others are more than sufficient reasons (reviewers should know that the necessary reasons are defined by the Law on University...) to propose Dr. Vojislav Seselj for election to the only, and at the same time, highest academic educational and scientific position, which he has had so far - the position of full professorship." Now, these words are, I think, attributed to the commission of which you were a part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may we take it that you, therefore, agree with these words?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. With everything that is stated here. I can affirm these words today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a Deputy Prime Minister, one of the five in the government of the day, was there for you, as for Vojislav Seselj, a joint responsibility for what you did, a shared responsibility for what you did?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you have in mind; within the cabinet, within the government? Well, within the cabinet, Mr. Seselj was in charge of economy, and I was in charge - and forgive me for having to repeat this so often - of legislation and legal system. Therefore, there was no cooperation between us as such. And now let me tell you this: When Mr. Seselj was appointed professor, I have to say that the room in which he lectured, there was not enough room for all the students who wanted to come in and listen to him. Students had to stand in the hallway in order to hear what he was saying. He's an excellent lecturer, and I can confirm once again, an excellent university professor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the government, it would not be proper or appropriate for any one of you five Deputy Prime Ministers to say something publicly that was outside government policy, would it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're trying to say. You come from a country which has a cabinet system of government. Those who disagree with the government's position resign from the cabinet. How can you be in the cabinet and not go along with what the cabinet is doing? If that is the case, then you are homo duplex. If you disagree, you have to resign. This is the rule of the cabinet system of government, which exists in Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By 1998, you had been involved with Kosovo, on your own account, for several years, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Unfortunately, not. I have to confess to you, and I believe that this is my own personal shame, that the first time I went to Kosovo was when I was sent there by the government. The first task I received from the government relating to Kosovo was on the 10th of March, 1998, when I was appointed head of a working group for negotiations with the representatives of political parties of Kosovo Albanians. That was the first time I was assigned a task related to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No doubt you became aware of government policy in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what policy you have in mind, what government policy in relation to Kosovo you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just simply generally. If you were being trusted with negotiations in Kosovo and then subsequently in 1999 you headed the delegation at Rambouillet over Kosovo, may we take it that you were informed of all aspects of government policy in relation to Kosovo? It would be hard for you not to be, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you followed closely my testimony, you could see that I was always tasked with issues that had to do with constitution and constitutional acts, and both of these things were included in negotiations with Kosovo Albanians and in Rambouillet, except that in Rambouillet, unfortunately, I was not given an opportunity to carry out that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, I understood you yesterday to say that you accepted a proposition, I think, that was put from a document attributed to you that it was the will of the people that mattered in the end when it came to constitutional issues, and that would presuppose that before you actually get down to drafting or amending a constitution, you need to know what the policy is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. That's what I said, that I could write a constitution for Zanzibar, too, if someone were to give me basic parameters for that constitution. A constitution, just like any other task, is a matter of trade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not then automatically follow that you must have been aware of what government policy was in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that's what I'm saying. I just would like Mr. Nice to tell me what policy he had in mind. I naturally know what the government policy is. I was Deputy Prime Minister, and I sat in all the meetings. But I have to say that there always was a Deputy Prime Minister in charge of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He'll get to that when he has a question to pose on that. His question was a general one which it to appeared to me simply demanded a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my final question on this topic is this: Did you become aware at any stage of any member of the government, whether a Deputy Prime Minister, Prime Minister, or whether this accused, Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, did you at any time become aware of anybody having kept back any aspect of policy on Kosovo from you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I couldn't say yes to that question of yours. I think that there existed a frankness among the cabinet members. Cabinet members constitute a team. We had very good relations among us in the government, and I don't think that anybody kept anything back from other members of the government. I am not aware of any secret meetings or any small teams within the government. All issues were discussed in plenaries, in government sessions, and there were various discussions, so-called coordinations, when some special issues in the field of economy were discussed. What I'm trying to say is that there were no secrets among the cabinet members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you, please, to look at a very short clip. It comes from 1998, and it will now be played to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's something wrong with the sound at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "NARRATOR: What Milosevic was trying to do next. "MR. SESELJ: [No interpretation]"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The transcript available for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that speech?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present at that rally, at that gathering. This was obviously a rally held outdoors, and I wasn't present. This must have been a rally of the Serbian Radical Party based on the people I see present on the stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here's the Deputy Prime Minister speaking, and he says in terms: "If NATO bombs us, no Albanians will be left in Kosovo." In light of what you've told us about collective responsibility of the government, in light of what you have revealed as the views of your commission on the quality of Mr. Seselj in academic and in all other ways, can you please tell us what was meant by a member of your government saying: "If NATO bombs, no Albanians will be left in Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cabinet was a coalition government. It wasn't homogenous in the terms of political parties. There were several representatives of several political parties. I did not belong to Mr. Seselj's party. He's a leader of the Serbian Radical Party, and I am a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia. Mr. Seselj uttered these words in his capacity as chairman of a political party. This was the position taken by his political party. He did not utter these words in his capacity as Deputy Prime Minister but, rather, as a party chairman. His political work has nothing, absolutely nothing to do with his academic qualities. It has nothing to do with that. We have to teach ourselves not to use anything else but scholarly parameters when writing these reports. We should absolutely ignore the party words and party work uttered by that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... actually answering, really, the question. Let me remind you what you said --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am answering your question, but it seems that my answer doesn't suit you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you was: What did he mean by saying: "If NATO bombs, no Albanians will be left in Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not Mr. Seselj's alter ego. You should put that question to him. How could I know what he had in mind when he uttered these words?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Remember what you told us about the duty to resign, and remember what you told us about the openness and frankness of government. "Frankness" is my word, I think, not yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But Mr. Nice, to be fair to him, he has also said that the cabinet was a coalition government, it wasn't homogenous, and Mr. Seselj was speaking not as Deputy Prime Minister but as leader of his Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but my question, if I may put it, is this:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Seselj ever criticised, sanctioned, or asked to resign because he had made what is a clear threat of what would happen to Kosovo Albanians if NATO bombed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should put that question to the Assembly deputies, because they are the only ones who can initiate a procedure of political accountability of a cabinet member. The Assembly deputies did not put on the agenda a no-confidence vote for Mr. Seselj. That procedure was never instituted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we turn to technicalities of the kind you've referred to, just remember all the answers you've given about being at the heart of government - my question - about the openness of government - your answer. What I want to know, what you can help the Court with is this: Did this accused or any other senior members of the government dissociate themselves from these words of Seselj?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how would I know that? These are personal issues. So you should put that question to each individual person. I cannot tell you what somebody else may think about something. You are attributing supernatural qualities to me which I do not possess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, then, that you are effectively saying - help me if I'm wrong - that you're not aware yourself of any action being taken against Seselj for saying what he did.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been only a no-confidence vote of the Deputy Prime Minister, and there was no such action taken. Prime Minister is not a teacher who can discipline somebody. The government, cabinet members, are appointed and removed from office by the parliament alone, and that can only be done by the parliament, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the Vreme article which the witness has adopted be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the video clip, the clip together with the transcript be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I raise opposition to that? We have a commentary on that video clip that is a statement as to what the accused was doing by whoever the journalist was - we don't know which journalist - and then a statement by Mr. Seselj, not adopted by this witness at all, knows nothing about it, and we're getting into more and more danger with exhibits in this form. If you look at this, the controversiality of the material that's being sought to be introduced in this way as an exhibit, it's not an exhibit of anything. It's got a statement within it about Mr. Milosevic's rejection of Rambouillet, what he was planning to do next, "nationalism had brought Milosevic to power, now it threatens to bring about his downfall --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not concerned about those passages. It's only the passage in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will just admit the quote attributed to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The article will be 820. The videotape will be 821. The transcript will be 821.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have, for various reasons, proceeded much more slowly than I had hoped. There remains the possibility of the Chamber, if it would accept it, reviewing Professor Kristan's observations on day one. They do start with some effective -- if it's not criticism, it's expressions of regret that he was apparently treated evidentially differently, but I'm sure the Chamber won't be offended by what he says. And the other document -- at least I hope it won't be, I'm sure it won't be. And the other document which at some stage I would like the Chamber to consider is the article that has been made available to the accused and that the witness had for his consideration by Slobodan Samardzic of the Institute of European Studies in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm concerned about what you're proposing in relation to Kristan, not because I value the 20 minutes of free time but because we haven't made a decision yet on to the extent to which, if any, he might be recalled. And indeed, we were considering whether that's something on which it might be appropriate for you to make a filing. We haven't made a decision on any aspect of that, we're just considering various possibilities. I see no harm in you putting propositions -- speaking for myself, I see no harm in you putting propositions to the witness that you may have derived from advice that you've got from Professor Kristan, but I think I feel at this moment uncomfortable about reading this in advance. There may be other circumstances where it's perfectly appropriate to read things in advance, but I'm uncomfortable at the moment. It may turn out that your suggestion was right, but I don't want to fall into a trap at this stage through the rush. Now, you can't be faulted for taking the time you've taken this morning, and indeed I personally think it important that points are clarified in this evidence. I'm anxious, for example, to hear just exactly what it is that was changed about the significant constitutions here about which there seems to be so much doubt and about which there should be certainty, and therefore if it's necessary to take time to do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that, then so be it. I would be unhappy to hear you protesting today that you are missing out significant elements of the evidence because there wasn't time to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll take all that into account. The only -- if I understand Your Honour's concerns, the advantage, if it were to be seen as a proper advantage of reading both of these articles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The article I have no problem with, it's the Kristan comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, is that it would enable me to present the somewhat detailed propositions in a much more efficient and quick way if everybody has pre-read, basically, my cross-examination. Now, if I were simply, for example, to take the name Kristan off the document - I haven't done this - and reduce it to a selection of 20 questions and asked the witness and the Chamber to review them in advance, that might have been acceptable, but I don't press it any further than that. That's the utility that I was seeking to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if I can say, the Kristan commentary, it's a commentary on the evidence of this witness. It's a highly unusual form of proceedings, receiving -- it could be a letter to the Judges saying, "This is what I think of this witness's evidence." There could be no end to this. It's a very dangerous and novel form, and we oppose that. The Samardzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's especially so, I think, Mr. Kay, because the basis on which he might be recalled is to give evidence of fact rather than expert evidence, and we haven't even decided how to categorise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Where it all leads is -- and the Samardzic article -- again, this is a very detailed text here, as I understand it. It's not an exhibit already in the case that you're being asked to look at because it's going to be put for cross-examination purposes to the witness. It's again a text by someone else that you're asked to look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we don't accept the invitation to read documents in advance in this way. Certainly the comments of Professor -- of Dr. Kristan on the testimony of Professor Markovic we will not hear. I entirely agree with Mr. Kay that it's dangerous. We don't know what it will lead to. You can seek to adduce the document by Slobodan Samardzic when we return. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please be given Samardzic's text in the Serbian language? I tried to. Did Professor Markovic get Samardzic in English or in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in Serbian. I got it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He got it in English. It's an English document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the rule of course applies, Mr. Nice, and you will have to put it on the ELMO and cite short passages. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, just so that the Chamber can remember the history of your functions, as well as being, as you say, an ordinary member of the SPS following your resignation from the Main Board, you were in fact also a member of the SFRY Assembly for a time, were you? Sorry, of the FRY Assembly.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I said. I was a member of the federal parliament, of the lower house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that from the beginning of the 1990s, when you were a founding member of the SPS and on its Main Board for a time, you were a member of the SPS, and you were either a member of the FRY Assembly or a Deputy Prime Minister, and that took you right the way through to 2000.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. As for political functions in the party, I lost them or, rather, I didn't have them from 1990 onwards, the end of 1990. So in 1992, I was elected federal MP on the SPS list, but I did not hold any party office. It was in 1994 that I became Deputy Prime Minister, and I ceased being a federal MP in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want your help in relation to Kosovo in this way: Evidence has been given before this Court, Professor Markovic, that some 1.45 million people were displaced, some 860.000 were forced to leave Kosovo, and some 10.000 Kosovo Albanians were killed. And the evidence -- it will be for the Court to decide, the evidence shows patterned use of special police forces and the VJ and systematic removal of papers of identification from those expelled. Can you please, from the heart of government, tell us what was the policy that led to that happening?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have to correct your mistakes yet again, because I cannot answer questions that are wrong. First of all, according to your math, Kosovo had a population of over 2.3 million. I think that you have exaggerated a lot. The actual population was at least a half of that. That is one matter. Secondly, as far as the government is concerned, the government policy, it always pursued a policy of seeking a political solution to Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say not to have an armed conflict but to have a political solution, and that is precisely why on the 10th of March, 1998, the delegation went there, in order to have political agreement reached and bloodshed prevented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be I didn't make myself clear, and I'm sorry if I didn't. I'm concerned with the suffering that happened in 1999, after the failure of Rambouillet, where you remained in office as a Deputy Prime Minister in a government that was transparent, as you explained it to us, so that you would know what was going on. Let's just deal with the 10.000 Albanians killed. What was the policy, please, of your government that led to that happening?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question has nothing to do with government policy. Of course the government did not pursue a policy of killing people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take another aspect of it. Forces eventually under the control of this accused, the army and others, systematically seized documents of identification from Kosovo Albanians numbering - and this is, incidentally, according to the UNHCR - some 860.000 forced out of their country. What, please, was your government's policy that led to that happening? Was it to expel all Albanians, or was it to achieve a dramatic change in the ethnic composition of Kosovo? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you. In the government I was in charge of legislation and the legal system. The government, at its sessions, and this is what you've been ascribing to the government, the government never pursued that kind of policy. The government had a policy that was the complete opposite. And I told you that in pursuit of that policy I went to Kosovo 15 times. However, obviously there was no wish to have this political settlement that we had proposed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember I asked you earlier whether in your judgement anything was ever kept away from you about policy in relation to Kosovo or generally, and you didn't identify ever being aware of things being hidden from you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if something had been hidden, I would have had to know that it had been hidden from me, but I am not aware of anything having been hidden away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, you dealt with Sainovic, didn't you? You dealt with the accused. You were trusted in the early stages to deal with all aspects of Rambouillet. Immediately following the failure of the Paris talks and the bombing started by NATO, Kosovo Albanians started dying and being expelled in large numbers. Can you explain it for us at all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I could not have cooperated with the Prime Minister, Nikola Sainovic, because we had two completely different departments that we were in charge of. He is an engineer. He was in charge of the economy. I am a lawyer, and on the republican government I was in charge of the legislation. We were on the delegation in Rambouillet, but as you saw, this delegation had a total of 12 numbers and the head of the delegation. So he was one of the members of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last two questions on this topic are these: Your fellow Deputy Prime Minister made it clear that if there was bombing, Albanians would suffer. That was the policy of your government, and it was put into effect, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is your assertion, Mr. Nice. I told you a few moments ago that that was not right. Mr. Seselj certainly stated that in his capacity as leader of the Serb Radical Party. You saw him speaking at a rally, not at a government meeting. You would be right if you had shown him uttering these words at the government meeting. As for what political leaders stay in the street, they say all sorts of things in order to win votes because they are worried about the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
