utterances.text: You know perfectly well, Professor Markovic, that politicians in office can't divide up their public utterances from their responsible government utterances. What you've been saying, and you've said this several times, is nonsense, isn't it? Once you're a politician, you're responsible for what you say.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said applies to a one-party government, a homogenous government. A government cannot discipline political parties. Every political party has its own autonomy because it has another concern, that is the elections that are coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Professor Markovic, in previous question put by Mr. Nice, you're asked, I will quote: "Immediately following the failure of the Paris talks and the bombing started by NATO, Kosovo Albanians started dying and being expelled in large numbers. Can you explain it for us at all?" But I don't think I heard your answer to that question. Could you give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot give an answer because I don't know. I don't know. I submitted a report to parliament about the course of the Rambouillet and Paris negotiations, and the following evening the bombing started. What happened after that, well, you see, when the bombing was on, the government did not have sessions. The government was relocated because the government building was a target and it had been hit. Half of the building was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to see if I follow your answer to His Honour Judge Kwon. Here you are at the centre of government in one of the greatest crises Serbia has suffered, where the most treasured part of Serbia, if we are to believe the protestations of Serb politicians, is suffering a forced exodus of a majority of its, as you would say, Serb republic population, because the Kosovo Albanians are Serb republicans, on your understanding, and you cannot offer any explanation in the year 2005 for what happened? Is that your position, Professor Markovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have an explanation. Of course I have an explanation. Of course the people are going to flee from bombs. People try to save their lives. How many times was Kosovo bombed? We watched all of that. How many people left Belgrade, if you wish, and went to other countries? How many people made it possible for their children to go away to be safe, because you didn't know when a bomb would fall. Only around my own building three bombs fell, and also windows were being shattered and falling out of the Ministry of the Interior that is in the neighbourhood. People were fleeing in order to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, the truth is, as you revealed in your last answer to the accused when he was examining you, you are one of those Serbs who believes that Serbs' dignity is more important than the lives of others, and you know perfectly well that a policy was pursued by your government that led to the extreme suffering of Kosovo Albanians, and you're simply denying it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what you said, it seems that it was the Serb government that bombed the Albanians and that it bombed the population in general, that it was the Serbian government that did that. That is the only thing that can be inferred from your question. Who was it that bombed the country? Those are the ones who caused the loss of lives and the exodus, those who bombed the country. The government simply did not want to agree to that, to have a shameful occupation of the country and to succumb to an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go back in time now to where we were at the end of my questioning yesterday, and I'm going to try to deal with matters sequentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I will deal in some detail with all the constitutions so that we can become familiar with them to the extent necessary. I should make the point to the Court that the Prosecution, in dealing with them in detail, doesn't concede that the shape of any of the constitutions or the manner of their change necessarily affects the position in law at all, but it's been adduced by us as part of the general background, referred to in greater detail by the accused through his witnesses really for the purposes of good faith on his conduct of events, and to that extent we must deal with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right, Professor Markovic, that the amendments upon which you were engaged in 1989 were focused on denying the provinces veto rights?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the point of the amendments at all. I've already told you that the vast majority of these amendments had to do with the economy and a different constitutional concept of the economy and the delegate system. Only one out of a total of 41 amendments, only one amendment, amendment 47, has to deal with constitutional powers in the Republic of Serbia and denying the provinces the right of veto to changes of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here, and you can see it, of course, off a media website, a quotation of yours made in the year 2000 in March, where you explained that the provinces were not excluded from exercising constituent authority, they were only denied veto rights. You can see the quote if necessary, but -- and I'll just repeat it so that it can be on the transcript. "The provinces were not excluded from exercising constituent authority. They were only denied veto rights." Is that your explanation, at least in part, for what happened in 1989?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just presented the substance of amendment 47. I put it very briefly, because Mr. Robinson asked me to talk about amendment 47 in the briefest possible terms, so I referred to it in one sentence only. However, if you insist, I can explain amendment 47 to you. The autonomous provinces still take part in changing the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. However, in terms of their opinion of changes to the constitution, if it differs, then there would be a republican referendum. They can only ask for a referendum in the republic. They can only ask for the citizens themselves to vote in a referendum if the opinion of the province is not taken into account in relation to constitutional changes. I put it in the briefest possible terms out of respect for what Judge Robinson asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Move on. As you know, at the beginning of 1989, there was a strike of miners. The Kosovo politician Vllasi was arrested, and on the 27th of February, a state of emergency was declared by the Presidency; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I told you and I told the Court that I entered politics only in 1992. I know about all of this only as a reader of the newspapers. I do not have any firsthand knowledge about this. And of course a lot of time has gone by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were on the commission dealing with the amendments. Were you really not aware of circumstances surrounding the approval by the Kosovo parliament of those amendments when they were -- when that Assembly apparently dealt with them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the Constitutional Commission is an auxiliary working body of the Assembly. It is the government, the Presidency then of the Republic of Serbia, and the Assembly that pursue policy. The Constitutional Commission is one of the commissions or, rather, auxiliary working bodies. You are giving the Constitutional Commission some kind of importance that it never really had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've asked you about the state of emergency, and I note that in your own proposed exhibits one that was not produced yet was tab 38, which is the confirmation by the Assembly of the SFRY of the state of emergency. Perhaps you'd just like to remind yourself of that, coming your way. We can provide a copy if that makes it quicker. Perhaps it has been admitted. What we see here is the Assembly supports the measures of the Presidency, introduced -- you can see it on the screen under "Conclusions." You can see that, "The Assembly supports the special measures introduced by the Presidency ... These measures have been introduced to preserve and protect the territorial integrity and constitutional order of the SFRY, to secure the public order, peace, freedom of work and well-being of all citizens, as well in order to normalise the general state of affairs in Kosovo." So emergency powers granted and by the time these amendments were dealt with, they were dealt with first in Vojvodina, I think, on the 10th of January, and they were then dealt with in -- I beg your pardon, on the 10th of March, and then they were dealt with in Kosovo on the 23rd of March. You must have been following, as an interested member of the commission, the question whether these amendments would be passed in Kosovo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The amendments were adopted in the parliament of Kosovo with a required majority, a two-thirds majority.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This tab 38, these are conclusions of the Assembly of Yugoslavia. If I remember correctly, if my memory serves me well, this was admitted into evidence during the examination-in-chief. Professor Markovic even answered questions in relation to these conclusions of the Assembly of Yugoslavia. The assessment of the changes in Serbia was a very favourable one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for being so alert, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move to the amendments themselves, Professor Markovic, were you aware of the presence of threatening force in Kosovo in the form of tanks and helicopters pursuant to the special powers given under the emergency? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The consent given by Kosovo is then reflected at the final stage on the 28th of March in Belgrade, and if we could display on the overhead projector further pages from marked for identification Exhibit 818, at page 55. We will just look at three of the actual amendments, to one of which you have already referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 55 in English, and 54, if the witness wishes it, from this document in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So amendment 27 says this: "In the official and public use in the SR Serbia shall be the Serbo-Croatian language and its alphabets... "In Serbia, in the territories inhabited by individual nationalities, the Serbo-Croatian language and its alphabets and the languages of these nationalities and their alphabets shall be in equal official use, public use ..." And then the next paragraph: "The official and public use of the Cyrillic alphabet shall be prescribed ..." Then the next paragraph: "The provincial Constitutions shall specify, consistent with the present Constitution, that the languages of nationalities shall be in equal official and public use in the territories of the Autonomous Provinces." That's one of the amendments which changed the previous rule on language, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said; that the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia found, ruled, that in para 3 of this amendment, or point 3 of this amendment was in contravention with the federal constitution, the constitution of the federation. And it found only three such instances of contravention; when it came to language, when it came to real estate, and when it came to the election of electoral units in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we see what was proposed. What was intended to be applied to Kosovo here? There is another amendment that I don't have in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on to that, Mr. Nice, one part you didn't specifically draw attention to you is in the third paragraph of that amendment, where it says: "State agencies and organisations exercising public powers in the Socialist Republic of Serbia shall use the Cyrillic alphabet unless specified otherwise by republican statute in individual cases." Now, is that of any significance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain, first of all, Professor, why it was thought appropriate to compel the use of the Cyrillic alphabet in what you were dealing with as the unsatisfactory position of the province of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Kosovo. It says here the republican law shall determine when in public use -- when the Cyrillic alphabet is in public use. So it is the law that is to stipulate that, not the amendment. The law shall enforce such-and-such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was that intended to extend --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Constitutional Court ruled that that provision was in contravention to the constitution, and I have the views of the Constitutional Court about it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're concerned with what you and the others drafting these amendments were actually trying to achieve, so please help us with the question. Why was it thought appropriate to compel the use of the Cyrillic alphabet, no doubt included in Kosovo? Professor Markovic, please -- I know you've got to look at the text, but please help the Judges. Tell us, how was compelling the use of the Cyrillic alphabet going to help the circumstances in Kosovo where you had 95 per cent Kosovo Albanians? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise for having to look at the text, but I cannot rely on your quotes because you quoted erroneously several times from the constitution. So I have to take time to look at the actual text of the constitution. That's why I'm looking at this. But let me say simply why the Cyrillic alphabet. The Cyrillic alphabet is more widespread, although the Latin script was treated on a footing of equality and is taught in primary schools, the same as Cyrillic is taught. I don't know how it is that through an alphabet on script you can express nationalism and national disenfranchisement, if you want. So the Albanian language cannot be written, for example, in the Cyrillic script, with the Cyrillic alphabet. It has its own script. What we're talking about here is the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can be clear about this. Professor, could you tell us whether, before this amendment, only the Albanian language was used in offices in Kosovo? So the purpose of this amendment to use -- to let both of the languages be used in the official area? The second sentence of the fourth paragraph says that: "The autonomous provinces shall ensure the equality of the languages and alphabets of the nationalities and the Serbo-Croatian language and its alphabets." If you could help us with this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were used completely equally. Both languages were in equal use. The Cyrillic Latin script only refers to the Serbian language, because the Serbian language has two scripts or alphabets, the Cyrillic and the Latin. It doesn't mean repression of the Albanian language as an official language. It remained the official language. And when I refer to the decision of the Constitutional Court, that is one of its findings and what it criticises. He says that in this way, the use of the Latin script in state organisations or institutions or public institutions can only be determined, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but my question is in factual terms whether Serbo-Croatian language was used in offices in official areas in Kosovo before this amendment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was, Serbo-Croatian and Albanian on a footing of complete equality. We're just talking about the script here, not language; the alphabet or script and not language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why did you need this kind of amendment at that time when the Serbo-Croat is used in official areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I say, it only has to do with the alphabet, the script, not language. Quite simply, the mass of the population finds Cyrillic closer to them. For example, I write in the Cyrillic script. I find it easier, because we have become used to it, whereas the younger generations have become more -- better versed in the Latin script because you have foreign languages, of course. That's all the Latin script. So the younger generation tend to write in the Latin script whereas I in the older generation tend to write in the Cyrillic script, but this provision is in contravention to the federal constitution and that was the ruling of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, the sentence I mentioned and which I think Mr. Nice's question relates to is the one in the third paragraph which requires the state agencies and organisations to use only the Cyrillic alphabet in writing, unless specified otherwise by republican statute in individual cases. And I think I'm right in understanding, and I just want to be absolutely clear, that that's the passage which was held to be unconstitutional and that in fact if it hadn't been so, it would have enabled the Serbian republican authorities to insist on the use of Cyrillic alphabet only in the written work of the state agencies and organisations in Kosovo. And following on that, Mr. Nice is asking you why, why it was thought appropriate to do that when the bulk of the population were Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you to do your best to understand me. This provision relates to the Serbs, not the Albanians, because they were using their own language and their own script, their own alphabet. So in the official use for Albanians, you had the Albanian language. This targeted the Serbs alone, that is to say those using Serbian as the official language in the work of state organs. This did not relate in any way to the Albanians, because the Albanian language was on a footing of complete equality with the Serbian language in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not what it says, Professor. It says clearly that the official and public use of the Cyrillic alphabet shall be prescribed by republican statute, and state agencies and organisations in the Socialist Republic of Serbia shall use the Cyrillic alphabet, and that socialist republic includes Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But already in the following paragraph, as you say, para, we see a provision which is special in relation to the previous one, and it says the provincial constitution, in conformity with this constitution, shall establish the languages of the ethnic groups on the territory of the autonomous province. So take the provisional constitution and you will see that Albanian was completely equal to the Serbian language. And let me repeat once again, para 3 refers exclusively to those people speaking Serbian, not the people speaking the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I think what Judge Bonomy was asking was where is that gathered from the text? Is it a matter of interpretation? Could you explain? It's certainly not explicit in the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can't have it in that text. You can have it in the constitution of Kosovo. That's where it will be, and that's where it states that, in the constitution of Kosovo, whereas these are amendments to the constitution of Serbia. And it says the provincial constitutions shall specify which languages of nationalities shall be in equal official and public use. Take the constitution of Kosovo and you'll see what it says, because legal norms are systemically expressed. You can't draw your conclusions about the whole on the basis of a single part. You must look at the whole together. And for official languages in Kosovo and Metohija, it is the constitutional -- the provincial constitution that specifies that, not this one, the constitution of Serbia. And this is the result of the social set-up of the Republic of Serbia itself. That was the system that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is interesting to observe also, Professor, that in the next paragraph, where reference is made to the provincial constitutions, that they have to specify that the languages - not the languages and alphabets but the languages - of nationalities shall be in equal official and public use, and that they have only to ensure the equality of the languages and alphabets of the nationalities and the Serbo-Croatian language and its alphabets without reference to use in public -- rather, in official and public organisations. However, I need take no more of your time on this, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now turn to one other of only two other amendments I need touch on. I don't have an English translation of this. It can be found in Defence tab 17 as one of the untranslated parts of the Official Gazette. So if we can simply place on the overhead projector what is, top left-hand corner, page 600 of this Cyrillic text of defendant's tab 17 and look at amendment 43, but for the usher it's the top right-hand part of this page, which is amendment 43, subparagraph 3. Can you confirm for us, Professor, that this amendment gave power to the President of Serbia to empower republican bodies to take over provincial organs in certain circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again a correction. The president of the republic did not exist pursuant to this constitution. It was only with the 1990 constitution that this existed. What existed was the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia as a collegiate organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbian Presidency could empower republican bodies to take over provincial organs; yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, when we're talking about this particular function, because the view was taken, and I've already explained this in response to the questions asked, that this was a function which is an eminently state function of interest to the republic as a whole and, therefore, its functioning as a whole cannot be left to the provinces themselves. So it is a state function. And I'd really like to hear any autonomous unit in the world having competencies in this sphere. It's a state function, a state empowerment linked to the state, and it was the Republic of Serbia that enjoyed statehood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by this measure, the potential for centralisation of the Serbian state was enhanced, wasn't it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree at all with that. Why centralisation? Why the centralisation of the state? Things are being brought back to the norm, the normal. The state is exerting its state functions. You can't have a province or municipality performing something that is only -- that is only the state that should be empowered to do. We know which functions the state carries out, what a territorial unit is and what a unit of local self-government is and what they are empowered to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third amendment is the one you've already dealt with, 47. Amendment 47, Article 3, which is contained in tab 17, we needn't look at it again, which withdraws Kosovo's -- province of Kosovo's veto power over changes in the constitution. Now, when these amendments were promulgated, it was not made clear, was it, Professor, the degree to which they were going to be used and extended and, in particular, it wasn't made clear that the Constitutional Court was going to be wound up, that the Assembly was going to be wound up, and so on. None of that was made clear to those listening to whatever public debate there was.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what your question is. What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, to your knowledge, in the public debate such as there was, was it ever made clear that there was going to be the use of these amendments basically to wind up Kosovo altogether; to take away the Assembly, to take away the Constitutional Court, to take away the Academy of Arts and Sciences, to take away the Institute of Kosovo History. Was any of that made clear by those of you who were promulgating these amendments?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of that is correct. None of what you're saying now is correct. These amendments did not take away any of those things. They continued to enjoy what they had before; the Constitutional Court and the Presidency and the provincial Executive Council and a provincial Assembly and their own Supreme Court and constitution and their laws and provisions. Where do you get this idea from at all that they lost and forfeited all that through the amendments? No. They retained it all through the amendments. The only thing they forfeited was the veto to the republican constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My earlier suggestion that you justify these amendments on the grounds that they were denied only the veto may be in fact your position. Is it your position that withdrawing the veto is what justified these amendments?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. How do you mean justified these amendments? There were 41 amendments. There were 41 amendments in all. This amendment is just one of these 41 amendments. So I don't know what you want me to say. What do you want to hear from me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on and come back to it. You will remember that on the 28th of June, 1989, 500th anniversary of the great loss of the Serbs at Kosovo Polje, the accused made his famous speech. Were you present? You can't have been because you've never been to Kosovo. No, in 1989 you had been to Kosovo. Were you present?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present at that meeting, and I say unfortunately so. Until I became vice-premier, I had never visited Kosovo at all. I say unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how these amendments perhaps took effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber would be good enough sticking with marked for identification number 818, which I'd be grateful if it could be placed on the overhead projector at page 57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will find that as early as July 1989, a couple of months, a few months after these amendments, this is what's done -- and in your case, Professor, the document concerned can be found on page 56. "The law on the restriction of real property transactions. "Real property transactions between physical persons, and between physical and civil legal persons in the territory covering a part of the territory of Serbia within the territory of Vojvodina, shall be restricted for a period of 10 years ..." And then Article 3: "The commission formed by the Assembly of Serbia shall authorise a real property transaction specified in Article 1 of the present Law, upon being satisfied that the transaction will not result in a change of the national structure of the population or the emigration of members of a certain nation or nationality." Now, this law, was this something that could only be achieved following the amendments to the constitutions? This time it happens to be Vojvodina, but there was a similar one for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have the text in Serbian. I'm looking at it in English, and from this portion, I can't see if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 56.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Which page? Which page 56?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should have been placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry if you didn't have it. Page 56 for the witness, page 57 for the ELMO. There it is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what's the question? I have the text now in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This promulgated for Vojvodina and to restrict ordinary sales of property between individuals, would that have been possible without these 1989 amendments, or was it only possible to achieve this sort of a law for Vojvodina after the amendments?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These amendments were passed in March 1989 and I can't see when the law was passed, but at all events, and this is what I said on the first day of my testimony, the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia found that the provisions of the amendment to the constitution of Serbia limiting the real estate transactions was in contravention with the federal state. So it was the Constitutional Court which had provided the Assembly with its ruling and opinion that this provision of the amendment was in contravention to the constitution of the federal state. But I cannot see from this what date this law was enacted. I can just see that it says Official Gazette number 30/89. But I'm not a professional -- I'm not expert in the realm of real property transactions, real property laws, so I'd have to read the foregoing laws to see whether it was regulated in some other manner by the previous law in comparison to this law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is very simple: Amongst the objectives of the 1989 amendments was the objective of population or demographic control, and that's made as clear as day by the rapid introduction of an extraordinary restriction on the sale of property. It has nothing to do with vetoes, it has nothing to do with structure of constitutions; it has to do with demographic control. Isn't that right, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Constitutional Court stated that that was in contravention to the federal constitution. So what you're saying is something that was expressed in legal terms by the Constitutional Court. The Republic is duty-bound to do away with that contravention from its amendments in the way it is at variance to the federal constitution. Now, your explanations, everybody has the right to make their own conclusions because you go through your thought processes and you can interpret it any way you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next thing in date order that you can probably help us with is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have a copy of this. I can get it copy of it but I don't want to burden you too much with more paper. It's referred to in the document before you but it's only referred to in the commentary section on page 51.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In March of 1990 following these amendments, a programme was announced called the Programme for the Realisation of Peace, Freedom, Equality, Democracy, and Prosperity, and it was pursuant to that programme and under the amendments that various other laws were made. Am I right about that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say I just don't know. At that time - let me repeat again - I was just a university professor. I don't know. I wasn't a deputy at the time. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same document marked for identification 818, can we now go, in the English, to page 71, and in the version before the witness, please, if he could look at page 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was clearly -- this was another law introduced now in 1990. I can't give you the precise date of this one, but it's the university law. There's an extract of it here. Paragraph 2: "In the socialist autonomous provinces, the syllabi shall also be followed in the language of another nation and nationality when not less than 30 students of the same year of study so opt." Incidentally, I must correct myself. I misspoke in saying 95 per cent Kosovo Albanians. I think the figures are 85 per cent or down to 82 per cent of Albanians in Kosovo at the time. With those figures in mind, this law would make it possible in the universities -- or the university in Kosovo for courses to be followed in Albanian if and only if not less than 30 students of the same year in a particular syllabus, I understand it, so opt. What do you say about that, Professor Markovic? What good is that going to do the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this provision was formulated for the following reasons: You know, much time is needed. Many efforts and much talent is needed in order to become a professor at a university. There simply wasn't enough qualified personnel able to teach in Albanian, and I know that for certain subjects there were absolutely no Albanian teachers. In order to become a university professor, you first have to have your master's degree, your Ph.D., and to write a number of publications from the relevant field. Therefore, it was very difficult all of a sudden to staff these positions with qualified personnel. Kosovo and Metohija is not a large territory, the number of qualified personnel is limited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interrupt you. How long had Pristina University been in existence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've really got me. I couldn't say, although I think that initially it was a department of the Belgrade law school, and when it became a full-fledged university, to my shame, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it was in the 1960s, I must suggest to you, and just help the Judges, please; what language was being used to teach the students up and until the 1989 amendments?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know. I never lectured at the Pristina University. I was never a visiting professor there either. To this day I've never given a lecture at the Pristina University. I only once attended a doctoral dissertation, and that was on the 16th of January, 1999. I remember this date. That was my sole involvement with the Pristina University. Certain of my colleagues did go there, and for my subject, constitutional law, there were lecturers who taught both in Serbian and Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how come then you offer this answer that there was an insufficiency of Albanian teachers? How can you possibly say that that's the reason for this law if your ignorance of what happened in this university is what you claim it to be? I mean, I'll find out and present one way or another the history of language use in Pristina University as soon as I can offer it authoritatively, but just answer us how could you give that answer, Professor, if you knew nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I supposed, I supposed that was so. If you want me to give you answers only about issues that I am certain about, then I would have to be silent, I would have to remain silent in relation to many of your questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the next provision on the same page; 70 for you, 71 for us. "The law on the termination of work of the Assembly of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo and the Executive Council of the Assembly of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo. "Proceeding from the fact that the Assembly of Kosovo has not functioned for a long period of time, that it has failed to comply with the constitution, and that the work of a large number of delegates of the Assembly of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo, and the majority of the members of the Executive Council of the Assembly of the province of Kosovo endangers the sovereignty, territorial integrity and the constitutional order of Serbia, the Assembly of Kosovo, the Executive Council of the Assembly shall terminate their work." And then under Article 2: "The rights and duties of the Assembly shall be taken over by the Assembly of Serbia, and those of the Executive Council of the Assembly by the Executive Council of the Assembly of Serbia pending a constitution of the new Assembly of Kosovo and the Executive Council of the Assembly of Kosovo." Under Article 5, a few lines down, we see that, "Deputies shall be relieved of office." This was a way of using the new powers of the amendments to make laws like this simply to take over everything in Kosovo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's absolutely untrue. The amendments were not a legal basis for this. This happened when the constitutional declaration was adopted proclaiming Kosovo a federal unit, upon the adoption of the Kacanik constitution. Similarly to what was done by Great Britain in '73 after the unrest in Londonderry. Absolutely the same thing happened; they suspended autonomy in Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to suspension, reinstatement of the Council and Assembly required elections. Can you help us, please, with when those elections were allowed to happen, if ever?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That never happened for the simple reason that part of Kosovo Albanians believed that they received their state, the state of Kosovo, through the Kacanik constitution and that all organs ought to be established in accordance with that constitution, not in accordance with the law of the Republic of Serbia. As far as I know, all agencies envisaged in Kacanik constitution were constituted pursuant to that constitution. So back then, they already considered that they had nothing to do with the Republic of Serbia and that the laws of Serbia were invalid in that territory. This was not the belief held by all of the Albanians, as I said, only by part of the Albanians. Through this mechanism, Mr. Rugova also became president of Kosovo. Not pursuant to the constitution of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo but pursuant to the Kacanik constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, your government never offered elections for the reinstatement or the establishment of the Kosovo Assembly, did it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the elections were boycotted by the Albanian population, and they constitute majority in Kosovo. Therefore, the elections never had a chance to succeed and to lead to the Kosovo agencies being established, because Albanian population refused to participate in these elections, and they constitute the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, was this legislation, the law on the termination of the work of the Assembly, possible even without the amendment of constitution in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was possible to realise that without the 1989 constitution. Additionally, this law was reviewed by the Constitutional Court of Serbia to assess its constitutionality. I explained to you what happened with the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. It ceased to exist when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's constitution was adopted on the 27th of February. No, I apologise, 27th of April, 1992. Prior to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I have the answer. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Give me one minute. I'll just check a reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at one other law made at about the same time, and it's at page 63 of the same marked for exhibit, 818, and this is at page 63 in the English and 62 in the Serbian. "To ensure --" if we put it on the overhead projector, please, at the top. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "To ensure constitutionality and legality, democratic freedoms and rights, duties and responsibilities of citizens and their equality throughout the territory of Serbia, the republican agencies, the Supreme Court of Serbia, the Office of Public Attorney of Serbia, the Republican Public Prosecutor, the Republican Social Attorney of self-management and the Court of Associated Labour of Serbia and the higher Business Court, (hereinafter republican agencies) shall have the right and duty to act in conformity with the provisions of the present law when so necessitated by reasons of security (special circumstances) in a part of the territory of Serbia." This gave enormously wide-ranging powers to all those identified bodies to act in Kosovo, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where you are reading this, to act in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It speaks of an ability of those bodies or individuals to work throughout the territory of Serbia, and by reason of the amendments, if for no other reason, unambiguously Kosovo now falls within Serbia. So enormous powers were given. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Kosovo always fell within Serbia. It was always within the composition of Serbia. How come you state that it started falling within Serbia after 1989? It was always within Serbia, even in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. And it was only in 1945 that it was given an administrative -- separate administrative identity. I cannot answer the question which is incorrect. I cannot. I am a university professor, after all; I do not want to disgrace myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I observe your answer, and perhaps you'd do me the courtesy, Professor Markovic, as you read English, perhaps you would -- have you got the English display of the question on the screen before you? Professor Markovic, have you? Because since you make a point, I'm just going to read you again what I said. "It speaks of an ability of those bodies or individuals to work throughout the territory of Serbia and by reason of the amendments, if for no other reason, unambiguously Kosovo now falls within Serbia." I wasn't excluding that Kosovo was a historical part of Serbia. I was simply saying that the amendments made this absolutely unambiguous. Now, perhaps you'd answer the question. Did this law give enormous powers to Serbian individuals and bodies?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a law that exists in every country, the law regulating the so-called extraordinary special circumstances. Therefore, these powers given to the republican organs should not be linked only to Kosovo, because these powers could be implemented in Vranje, in Kikinda, in any other part of Serbia. Why are you coming out with this attitude that all of this was directed only to Kosovo? This law applied in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Leskovac?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. However, we did have special circumstances, law applied in the Republic of Serbia recently. This law could not have been applied in Kosovo. This law is only applied in places where special circumstances exist. Every country in the world has laws of this nature, the so-called laws that regulate extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you're at a convenient point, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I can simply say that we'll be turning to how these laws were - and similar - were applied later. The major exercises I must do are to take the Court through the relevant parts of and criticisms and comments on the 1990, the 1992 constitution. I must also deal with the account of Rambouillet, and I shall not be able to conclude this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just be sure. You will not be able to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform the Chamber of the fact that I've been here for 15 days now. Now it seems likely that I would have to remain here. I have an operation scheduled in Belgrade. I never expected that it would be necessary for me to remain in a foreign country this long in order to testify. It is simply impossible for me to be absent from my country and from my duties there for which I receive remuneration this long. It is exactly 15 days today that I've been away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that a medical operation that you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was that scheduled for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely because of The Hague, I postponed my surgery, and the surgery has been scheduled immediately upon -- was scheduled immediately upon my return. I have certain medical problems. I was supposed to have this surgery before I travelled to The Hague, and it seems, though, there is no end in view of my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot -- I had expressed the view earlier that I'd like to conclude the evidence, especially in light of one or two of the answers of the witness, but time has passed. These matters are important and detailed. The accused has made more significance of the statutes as part of his Defence. I regard it as essential now that I take the Chamber through the four constitutions and the family that we need to look at and deal with the other evidence, and I cannot properly conclude the evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're entitled to, Mr. Nice, but we have to be sensitive to the professor's obligations and in particular to his medical condition. Let us consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, the likelihood is that the furthest that you would have to remain here for testimony would be Monday morning, maybe by the end of the first session, which is 10.30. It will be either that or you would be required to come back at some date later. You didn't tell us the precise date of the operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The surgery will take place immediately upon my return from The Hague. I was supposed to have the surgery before I came here. Your officials are informed of all my medical problems. They have witnessed them. In that case, if I should have to remain here until Monday, then could please my flight be scheduled for Monday afternoon? Could I please take the first flight that leaves after that? I am aware of all the expenses the Court has incurred with respect to my stay here. I think that I am the witness who has had to stay the longest here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, but it's in the international public interest. I believe the Victims and Witnesses Unit would be able to arrange for you to leave the earliest flight after the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must be candid that the amount of detail that I have to go through, and I'm anxious to get on with it, may make that optimistic. I also know that it is possible to take both early and late afternoon flights to Belgrade, because I've done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, would a flight in the late afternoon, would that also be all right? It would still be on Monday but later in the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when the flights leave for Belgrade on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we can have that information before the end of the session. Mr. Nice -- or the Court Registrar, would you get that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I return to questioning the witness, I'm asked to make a correction to something that appeared - nothing to do with this witness - in our public January the 6th filing, where it was asserted that this trial is broadcast live on RTS Belgrade. That was incorrect. It's channel B92 that broadcasts the trial, and RTS has asked us to make that correction, and I happily do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, by June of 1990, SPS is formed, and there was an address by the accused to the Serbian Assembly on the 25th of June where he dealt with the question of borders. Were you present, by any chance, at that Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, because I was not a deputy at the time. And I have to make a correction once again. The SPS was not founded in June but, rather, in July. On the 16th of July, not in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No doubt there were preliminary meetings. Were you party to those meetings if you were on the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have been on the Main Board only after the SPS was founded, and the SPS was founded in July, not in June. Your question pertains to June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware that the programmes written by Mihailo Markovic dealt with the existence of autonomous regions for Serbs out of Serbia. Were you aware of that? You've heard about those from him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm somewhat skeptical with respect to the claims that one person wrote the entire document. Similarly, you attributed an entire constitution to me. It was a collective work project. It wasn't done by Academician Markovic alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We only have his evidence to go on, and take as long with the answers as you like, but I'm trying to deal with matters quickly. The question is: Are you aware that the programmes dealt with the existence of autonomous regions for Serbs out of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would be so kind as to tell me what the programmes specify, then I could answer. Otherwise, I'm unable to answer. I cannot be expected to know the contents of the programme by heart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If necessary, I'll come back to it. I can't take time in view of the pressures. Of this will be aware: In the summer of 1990, there was the log revolution, particularly in Knin, having, amongst other effects, for example, cutting off the Zagreb to Zadar road. And we've heard evidence of the arming of Serbs at that time. Two questions: If those things happened, do you - and we're going to be looking at your writings on these topics later - do you accept that to use logs to disrupt a state and movement through a state, do you accept that that is the application of force?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand, through that mechanism the Serbs in Croatia expressed their will, namely that they did not wish to leave Yugoslavia. They wanted to remain where they were, in the state in which they were. They did not want to be taken out of that state by way of a secessionist act of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you answer the question: Is that an act of force?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert for those matters. How could I be expected to answer that, whether it was an act of force to place a log? There were all kinds of demonstrations in Belgrade taking place all the time that disrupted the traffic. I don't think that I could call that an act of force. It's an act of protest because of something, and the citizens are entitled to protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's your answer. If, as the evidence has been, Serbs in Croatia - that is not army, not police; ordinary Serbs - were provided with firearms, is that an act preparatory to violence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could I know that, Mr. Nice? At that time, as I keep telling you, I did not have any such knowledge. I don't know about that. If you go on asking me this kind of questions, you can go on for a fortnight. I did not take part in this at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you want to comment, it takes time. Can we now move on chronologically to June of 1990. I want you to look at a document which I have in a short form and a long form. It's in English. It will be laid on the overhead projector and made available to the Court. It's headed "Discriminatory and unconstitutional laws and other judicial acts on Kosovo passed by the Assembly of Serbia," and I want it to see if you can help me, and if you can't today you may be able to over the weekend, with some facts asserted in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in English, so it will have to go on the overhead projector. And it's the last page of this document, if you would be so good, Usher. I can't get a display at the moment. Can we have the overhead projector, please, displayed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Left-hand side, towards the bottom of the page, and this is now up to the 27th of June, so just before your arriving on the scene as an SPS member, it says this, immediately under the bolded words "Official Gazette of SPK": "On the occasion of granting such an unconstitutional consent, upon the initiative of Academician Gazmend Zajmi and lawyer Bajram Kelmendi, the Constitutional Court of Kosovo with its verdict numbered on the 27th of June, 1990, decided to initiate a procedure to assess the constitutionality of the Assembly of the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo in giving consent for the amendments 9-49 of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia of 23 March. The Court Council consisted of..." and then the Judges are listed. "By a project decision of the Court, numbered, of the 27th of July, the decision to give consent to the amendments in the constitution of Serbia was annulled and the Constitutional Court Council consisted of the following Judges," named. "The verdict remained unsigned, for in the meantime, the Assembly of Serbia, after it had introduced a state of emergency to Kosovo, also in an unconstitutional way passed another unconstitutional law on the cessation of work of the Assembly of Kosovo, its executive body, and other officials." Now, you're the constitutional lawyer. You were party to the introduction of these amendments. This document suggests that a proper complaint to the Kosovo Constitutional Court was brought, was successful in that the amendments were annulled, but it all came to nothing because Serbia erased the Court, cut the Court out, killed the Court. Is that right, factually? Because you haven't told us about it in your own evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this quotation, the question was not put very specifically. I see now what Mr. Nice has -- by a project decision. That's what it says here. So it was not an actual decision that was taken, it was a project decision, a draft decision. It was not a decision that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, and stop trying to rehearse him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whatever a project decision is, the witness can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not the first time, if I may say so, Your Honour, that the interventions of this accused may have had the effect and it may be have had the purpose of alerting witnesses to answers they can give. I read out quite precisely and intentionally "project decision" in order that this witness can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The constitutionality of the change of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia cannot be reviewed by the Constitutional Court of Kosovo and Metohija. They can only review the constitutionality and legality of the laws of Kosovo and Metohija. As for the laws and constitution of the Republic of Serbia, it is only the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Serbia that can review those. Therefore, they usurped a right. They did not act within their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. jurisdiction. It would be as if a federal unit was reviewing the constitutionality of the federal constitution. How could that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, that's -- misrepresents what's said here. The issue was the constitutionality of the act of the Kosovo Assembly, not -- they weren't attacking or challenging some act of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the Assembly of Kosovo agreed to the amendments to the republic constitution. The Constitutional Court cannot rule on actions. It can only rule on legal documents, that is to say the constitutionality of adopting amendments, constitutional amendments. That is so-called formal constitutionality. And it is not the Constitutional Court of Kosovo that is in charge of doing that but the Constitutional Court of Serbia. I already explained to you at the very beginning that the Constitutional Court is reviewing only the constitutionality and legality of general legal acts and legal documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now will you answer, if you'd be so good, Professor, my question and not a question of your own creation, because that's what you did. My question was: Is it factually correct that complaint about the consent was taken to the Kosovo Constitutional Court and that by a project decision it was annulled but that the matter couldn't be taken further because the Constitutional Court was itself wiped out? Is that factually accurate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to the first question is I don't know; and the second, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll press on from that. We know just with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if it is not factually correct, I'm interested in knowing what the correct -- what is the accurate statement. What is the correct position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I was not a judge on the Constitutional Court of Kosovo. I don't know at all whether there was any kind of proposal before the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia to assess constitutionality and legality. I was a judge on the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia in 1991. I only became one in 1991. I cannot have an overview of all the cases before all the Constitutional Courts of Yugoslavia because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So then your answer to the second question should have been, "I don't know." No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, my answer to the first question was I don't know. I don't know that proceedings were initiated before the Constitutional Court of Kosovo. I don't know. And as for the second question, I said that it is not correct. That is to say the Constitutional Court of Kosovo was still there. I don't know the facts, but I do know the law. The Constitutional Court of Kosovo continued to exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, and I'm not going to trouble you with the document, I can't find it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it may be that the -- to clarify that point, a little further down in the same passage, it says -- it ends, that paragraph: "So a moratorium in the work of the Constitutional Court of Kosovo ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ensued, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "... and immediately after that this institution likewise ceased to exist." So, Professor, you're technically saying, then, that the Constitutional Court, at that particular time, was still in existence because it was in the stage which is described here as a moratorium; it had not yet ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court existed -- the Constitutional Court of Kosovo existed until the constitution of the Republic of Serbia entered into force on the 20th of September, 1990. That is when a completely different organisation was envisaged for the province. The province had three types of organs; a provincial Assembly, a provincial Executive Council, and provincial agencies. And from 1990 onwards, it no longer had a Constitutional Court because it no longer had a constitution. From then on, it had a statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All these things will be made clear ultimately. Go ahead, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And incidentally, I'm reading from the same article at the top left-hand side, the general alleged history, which we've had in evidential form. I'll just ask the professor this as a constitutional lawyer: One of the things noted and probably complained of to the Kosovo Assembly -- to the Kosovo Constitutional Court was that on an important matter like this, the effective voluntary surrender of all their autonomy by the Kosovo Albanians, the vote wasn't counted and there was no listing and identification of those voting. Do you as a constitutional lawyer think that's a good way to carry on; not to have a proper count of votes on a matter of this extreme importance?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are proceeding from a premise that is completely wrong. Again you're talking about surrendering an autonomy. There was no surrender of autonomy. How many times do I have to say that? In 1989, it was not the autonomy of either Vojvodina or Kosovo that was suspended. I just explained this. There were only five amendments that pertained to autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For these five amendments, these five little amendments with the consequences that we're going to see, do you think it was a good idea to have counted the votes and to have listed those present as being qualified to vote? Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The question really should be whether he knows whether the votes were counted or not in the first place. This is a comment being dressed up as a question and is unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it's not, because the evidence is quite clear, because the Defence has shown the video of the vote and it has been uncontroversial that there was no counting of the votes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think he can answer the question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not able to answer the question because I was not present physically. I am bound by my solemn declaration to speak the truth. How can I talk about this when I was not present? You had Mr. Jokanovic here as a witness, who was actually present there. I was not. I was in Belgrade. How could I know what the session of the Assembly of Kosovo went? I didn't even watch it on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's the question you've been asked, Professor. You've been asked whether, if the votes were not counted, and there is evidence suggesting that, whether if that happened, that was an appropriate way to proceed in something as important as this; and you're being asked that as a constitutional -- professor of constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need to be a professor of constitutional law in order to be able to answer that question. Of course in that case it would not be an appropriate way to vote, but I'm speaking in completely abstract terms. I don't know what the situation was in the Assembly of Kosovo, whether they did the counting or not. But of course, if the votes were not counted, then there can be no decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move straight now to the Serb constitution of September 1990. It's, I think, tab 16, but we've got it in full. Forget that. Withdraw that. We've got it in full. And the document itself has been exhibited as Exhibit 319, tab 1, or Exhibit 132, but I'll display the relevant passages on the overhead projector and ask for the witness's comments. Can the witness have the Serb version? I'm sorry, I haven't done complete connections between the various pages, but it may be my colleague will be able to take me straight away to the connecting pages if we've got the B/C/S version here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a document that was published, Professor, with the advantage of a preamble written by yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who wrote the preamble?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Constitutional Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have a look, then, at the document we have in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The page numbers, Usher, are on the bottom of the page. The first page we'd better look at is page 9, which is the end of the preamble. We don't have it in the B/C/S, I'm afraid, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's an introduction, and it seems to be signed by yourself, Dr. Ratko Markovic, Professor at the University of Belgrade. We can see that. And if we come to the first page of this document, which has got page 3 at the foot of it. If the usher would be so good. It is the beginning of the document, apparently signed by yourself, and it begins: "By means of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 1990, after many years, the dignity is being returned in the entire Yugoslavia to the constitution as a legal act." Before we move on at all, in a document that in the way we have it has sequential ERN numbers, do you remember writing this either introduction or preamble to this constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what I have before me is the constitution of the Republic of Serbia and the preamble to that constitution. Where do you get the idea that the preamble is written by an individual? The preamble is an integral part of the constitution. It precedes the constitution. It would certainly not be truthful if I were to say that I wrote the preamble. I don't know what this is that I signed. Why don't you tell me, what document is this that I signed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... constructive with our use of time. I've shown you your signature at the end of a document of six pages, starting at page 3. It's then continuous through to page 9. Can you help us; if it wasn't a preamble, was it a preface, was it an introduction? What was it that you signed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should know what it was that I signed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you identify the document? I cannot find it among the exhibits here. What document is this? I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can find it at tab 16. In English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is translated as "Preface".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, now I understand. Mr. Nice, you do not distinguish between a preamble, which is an integral part of the constitution, and the preface that is written by the author. And you say that the preface is an integral part of the constitution. This is an authored piece of work, whereas the preamble is an integral part of the constitution. For the umpteenth time, you've put the question wrongly. The preface is written by the author, whereas the preamble is an official document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you and I'm going to ask you this question: Are you by your answers where you keep suggesting that I'm making errors trying to distract attention from matters in hand? Is that what you're doing? Because you do it so often that I'm suggesting to you it has an oblique purpose. You're taking time. Is that what you're doing, trying to obfuscate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice, I can't accept that. There is a distinction between the preface and preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I gave him a number of opportunities, Your Honour, if it wasn't a preamble, whether it was an introduction and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has made a point. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, Usher, please go to the bottom of page 4 in English, and the Cyrillic version will be coming downstairs in a couple of minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the foot of page 4, last paragraph, it says this, fourth line down: "Contrary to constitutional definitions of multinational states - independent or federal units - both in the world and in our country, the constitution of Serbia does not define the state by applying the ethnic criterion (a state of the Serbian people) but by applying the democratic criterion of a national, namely citizen sovereignty (a state of all citizens living within it)." That's your understanding of the position of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the definition of Serbia from Article 1 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, where Serbia was defined through the sovereignty of citizens, not the sovereignty of a nation. It is the citizens that are the mainstay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must be me alone that's confused about this, but I thought a large part of your evidence was to the effect that Serbia wasn't a state at this stage at all and that it was Yugoslavia that was the state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yugoslavia was the federal state, a federal state. And in Article 3 of the constitution of the SFRY from 1974, republics are defined as states. Therefore, the Republic of Serbia is also defined as a state in the 1974 constitution. But I can also tell you what -- how the provision actually reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Usher, page 7 at the bottom, please. Middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "According to the new constitution of Serbia, only one state does exist, as everywhere in the world, in the territory of the single state of Serbia. This, as something entirely natural, should not be emphasised at all, but the fact is that until now, due to the asymmetric state order of Serbia, three states have been in existence in its territory, namely two provincial ones and, between them, the third one which was a state the least. In the constitutional order of Serbia, there still are autonomous provinces, but now as units of territorial autonomy, such as the provinces in Italy and autonomous communities in Spain. In other words, without state functions." Your new statute had as its purpose to remove any autonomy of function from the two provinces and to make a single centralised Serbian state; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which case, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me to give short answers, and now you're asking for a lengthy answer. But it is incorrect. That's not what it means. The autonomous provinces have an autonomy within their own sphere of activity. They are not states that have statehood. They do not have a judicial legislative executive power, only an autonomy like the autonomous provinces in Italy and in Spain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the position after the amendments. Shall we go to page 8, please, Usher, at the --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You're mistaken again, Mr. Nice. That was not the position after the amendments. I am sorry for correcting you, but I cannot give answers to questions that are wrong. Then it would seem that I were condoning the mistakes. This was in 1990, and you have to learn constitutional law if you want to put these kinds of questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The constitutional law of your country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom of page 8. Do you --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to constitution law in general, in general, and then the constitution law of my country, too. I can understand that there is a lack of knowledge of that, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Due to the present constitutional status of Serbia, the question Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. may arise as to whether Serbia with the new constitution has turned its back to the federal Yugoslavia. By the new constitution, Serb has only made more precise the character of its link with Yugoslavia. Serbia has entirely recognised the primacy of the federal constitution - until Yugoslavia continues to have the federal order. Some other non-federal Yugoslavia is beyond the political and state interest of Serbia. Precisely because of that, and due to the tendency of squandering the federal Yugoslavia which is now visible, Serbia had to include in its constitution the defensive clause --" and I'm not sure whether that's "too" or "100," but never mind. "A violation of the federal constitution at the detriment of Serbia entitles Serbia to self-defence. In such cases, namely republic authorities shall issue acts in order to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia. "The constitution of the Republic of Serbia enacted in 1990 has established in its constitutional norms a new society and a new state. Such qualitative changes of society and state are done in the world in revolutions where, as a rule, the blood is shed. The new constitution of Serbia has transformed the entire anatomy and physiognomy of the constitutional order of the Republic of Serbia without shedding a drop of blood. It marks a recision from the utopian constitutionality of the Kardelj type, while trying to build up democratic foundations of an entirely new society and state, based on well-known and verified clear democratic principles. This constitution opens, therefore, a new era of democratic constitutionality ..." That's the way you prefaced this constitution, acknowledging what, that Serbia was going to exert supremacy over the federal state if it so chose?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've made a mistake once again, and the proof of that pudding is in Article 135 in English. Article 135, which states quite the opposite to what you have said. Here is what the article says: "The rights and duties vested under the present constitution in the Republic of Serbia --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
