utterances.text: It's on page 57.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "[In English] -- which is part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which by the terms of the federal constitution are to be exercised in the federation shall be enforced in accordance with the federal constitution." [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you have distorted --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you read it out from my preface. "[In English] It acts of the agencies of the Federation or acts of the agencies of another republic, in contravention of the rights and duties it has under the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, violate the equality of the Republic of Serbia or in any other way threaten its interests, without providing for compensation, the Republic agencies shall issue acts to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This does not give Serbia the right to overrule the federal government, or purport to do so?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it is violating the federal constitution. It is a means of self-defence since the secession of Yugoslavia [as interpreted] was already underway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at some of the other provisions, if we may, that go to make this point good. If the usher would be good enough --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, the response by Mr. Markovic, it says "because it is overturning the constitution." He did not say violating the constitution, he said violating the federal constitution, and that's what it says in the text he read. So it is the federal constitution, violating the federal constitution. Only if there is violation of the federal constitution do protective -- are protective measures taken, et cetera. The Professor said federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can have page 32, and if you want to follow it in the original, Professor Markovic, it's Article 72, and I've got about six articles I want us to look at and that's all. "The following shall be regulated and provided by the Republic of Serbia: "Sovereignty --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you hold on a minute so that the Chamber could follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 21 of tab 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll start again. Article 72: "The following shall be regulated and provided by the Republic of Serbia: "Sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the Republic of Serbia and its international position and relations with other states and international organisations." Subparagraph 2: "Realisation and protection of freedoms and rights of man and citizen; constitutionality and legality." But then this, subparagraph 3: "Defence and security of the Republic of Serbia and of its citizens; measures to cope with the emergencies." Now, those are all functions of the republican government, aren't they, properly? Or the federal government, sorry, properly and here they are now being assumed by the Serbian government. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. What you say is not true. There's another error, and I'm looking at number 35. "The rights and duties vested under the present constitution in the Republic of Serbia [In English] which is part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which by the terms of the federal constitution are to be exercised in federation shall be enforced in accordance with the federal constitution." [Interpretation] Bear that in mind, please, Mr. Nice. Article 135, para 1 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, which states something quite different from the way Mr. Nice just put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just help me. We're going to find out in due course that Serbia established a Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a Ministry of Defence. How is that all justified if you're in a proper federation with Montenegro or anybody else? Because that's what you did -- or not you, of course, but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did happen and it went on for a very brief period. In the law governing ministries, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia and the Defence Ministry was abolished straight away and Montenegro still has a Foreign Ministry, albeit Serbia and Montenegro are a state community now. But while it was within federal Yugoslavia, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I mean, Montenegro always had a Ministry of Foreign Affairs regardless of the fact that it was within the federation, whereas the Republic of Serbia, when the first amendment on the law on ministries came about, it abolished the Ministry of Defence, the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SFRY still existed at the time you were drafting this document, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SFRY did exist in legal terms until the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Usher, and for you it's the end of Article 72, subparagraph 12. "Other relations of interest for the Republic of Serbia, in accordance with the constitution." Sorry, that's prefaced by regulated and provided by the Republic of Serbia. "The Republic of Serbia shall maintain relations with Serbs living outside the Republic of Serbia in order to preserve their national and cultural historical identity." Now, just tell us, please, what that was all about. Why would Serbia, which we've heard claimed in due course had nothing to do with the war, was never at war, why should it be setting out here an intention to preserve the national and cultural historical identity of Serbs living in, in particular, Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where did you read that, that it says Serbia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't. I'm just suggesting that to you. You tell us -- very well, Professor. You tell us, then, where were you maintaining relations with Serbs living outside the Republic of Serbia? As you will be able to recall, a ministry was formed for dealing with Serbs outside Serbia. Where did it have its offices? It had the offices in Belgrade, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But every state looks after its members, the members of its nation. So we're talking about the Serbs from Vancouver, Canada, the Serbs of Chicago, the Sydney Serbs. Why are you linking that to merely Serbs in Bosnia and Croat? Wherever there are Serbs living, their original organisation enables them to have their own specialties determined; culture, customs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we ever find the documents or find the time to explore the documents of that office for external relations, it's going to be focused almost exclusively on Bosnia and Croatia, isn't it? Quite simple. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 36, please, Usher. And article 83 for you, Professor Markovic. "President of the republic shall propose to the national assembly a candidate for the post of Prime Minister and hearing the opinion of the representative of the majority of the national assembly --" 2, 3 and then 4: "Conduct affairs in the sphere of relations between the Republic of Serbia and other states and international organisations in accordance with law." Just pausing there so that we can draw an analogy. Unless I've got it wrong. Is this like the state of Maryland in America having a Ministry of Foreign Affairs? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is about the president of the republic, and he is not the Foreign Minister if he's president of the republic. The president of the republic is the head of state, and by definition the head of state represents the country within the state and abroad, outside the country. So we're talking about differentiation here between the theoretical definition of a head of state, because we know what a head of state is, what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just answered His Honour Judge Bonomy on that. It wasn't a state, was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The republic. Well, let's look at the next bit.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just a moment, please. Don't put words in my mouth, words that I haven't said, Mr. Nice. Let's be decent here and civil. I said that pursuant to Article 3 of the SFRY constitution, the republic is a state. Take a look at article 3 of the SFRY constitution, the 1974 one. Why are you putting words into my mouth?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at article subparagraph 5. The president's now going to "command the armed forces in peacetime and in war, and the popular resistance in war under the general - something - partial mobilisation organise the preparations for something in accordance with law." What were the armed forces in Serbia that required the command of its president?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed force -- there were no armed forces in Serbia. Serbia never had any armed forces. But this constitution was written at the time when we saw secession taking place and when there was the danger of Serbia -- or, rather, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia be divided up into as many units as there were federal units. When the federal 1992 constitution came into being, these provisions on the armed forces ceased to be in force, and then we looked to the 1992 constitution. And you must bear in mind that when this particular constitution was passed, Yugoslavia was encountering an economic crisis. There were -- the republics were seceding, and Serbia had to make provision in case the republic seceded. So this was in force until the new constitution came into force. And there were no armed forces in Serbia. This is a defensive clause which in view of the circumstances was necessary and needed to be incorporated into the constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, you're quite right to correct me about paragraph 4 when I referred to a Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I should have, of course, referred to, in the analogy, the governor of Maryland, I suppose. Extending that analogy, if we can, it would be a very major step for the governor of a state such as Maryland to decide not only to have foreign affairs but to have its own armed forces and to command them in preparation for some dissolution of the federal arrangement. You've told us on more than one occasion that you were merely a technician doing your drafting, so will you tell us, please, who instructed you to make provision for Serbia to have, under the command of the president, armed forces? Who instructed you to make that quite extraordinary provision? While you're thinking about it, I'm going to make this proposition: There's no way that could have been your initiative, is there, Professor? Somebody had to tell you to do that. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Nice, you are linking the entire constitution to myself as the author. You would have to ask the entire Constitutional Commission that, because this text was adopted by the Constitutional Commission, whereas you keep ascribing me the authorship. I would become Leo Tolstoy in a few minutes in view of all the things that I have written. So I have given you an explanation as to why it says what it does say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, you must remember that in examination in chief you gave answers including answers about how good, effectively, and worthy and excellent this constitution was. You didn't claim any ignorance or non-responsibility for it then. Well, now it's the commission. Tell us, please, who instructed the commission to make this accused have responsibility for international relations and to have authority for command of an armed force?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These questions are quite improper, because they completely leave aside the answers given by Professor Markovic that nothing that the Yugoslav or, rather -- came under federal competency pursuant to this constitution held true but was that it was the constitution of Yugoslavia that was being applied. And he quoted Article 135. So this about the armed forces and all the rest of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I've stopped you because you're now descending into comment. We are coming to the break, and I cannot suffer another rap on the knuckles, because my fingers are sore. Just one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like an answer to the question that I put, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who gave you your drafting instructions? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood it, and the answer is just one word: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that I tendered that dealt with the possible history of the application to the Kosovo Constitutional Court, may it either be exhibited or exhibited marked for identification? The position is that I have found a complete version of that document which goes into alleged -- a longer list of alleged discriminatory acts and laws. On this topic, this witness is an expert, so he tells us, and if we can't find the source material for numbered decisions, it may be that he can do that over the weekend, because the decisions are fully identified and numbered and described, the one being a project decision. But I would ask that the document be exhibited at the moment, being no reason not to. And if there is any challenge to what I've said, the witness have an opportunity to return to it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. I wanted to come in in relation to the document that was produced from the Kosovo Information Centre. And we've had a chance to consider the practice during the first phase of the trial, the Prosecution case, when Mr. Milosevic was engaged in this exercise. His documents were actually returned to him, and he was told that his time would come to produce such documents, that there wasn't this wholesale practice of marking for identification. And if there is to be consistency in the approach to this matter - because this is quite plainly a controversial document written by someone who has not been a witness in the Prosecution case, not adopted by the Defence witness, and containing an entirely contrary proposition to the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adopt the same procedure as we did in relation to the earlier document. We'll mark it for identity and we'll later give a ruling on all of these documents. We have in mind the question of consistency. Of course, it is always better to be correct rather than consistent. We can't ignore what happened in the Prosecution case. Professor, I'm told that a flight will be available in the afternoon, late afternoon, at 6.00 p.m. on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there no earlier flight?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: None earlier, from what I understand from the Court Registrar. Perhaps something could be done about improving air links between Amsterdam and Belgrade, but it's not within my power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I should like to ask that a ticket be booked, then, so that I can go from the court to the airport straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and we thank you for your cooperation, Professor. We'll then resume on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I give the number to the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will be 822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Marked for identification, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
